title: Investigating the Early Signatures of Feature Learning in Deep Linear Networks
comment: 92 pages, 7 figures, 16 pages of main text
summary: Deep neural networks learn data-dependent features, a capacity widely credited for their empirical success. However, explicitly characterizing what features emerge -- and when they improve generalization -- is challenging, since training is nonlinear and non-convex and the data is often anisotropic. Here, we give a closed-form account of feature learning for a deep linear network in a mean-field parameterization, trained by one gradient step from initialization on high-dimensional data carrying a low-dimensional (spiked) signal. In the infinite-width mean-field limit, one step updates each layer's feature kernel by a target-aligned rank-one spike, amplified by both the learning rate and the layer depth. We next assess how these features impact prediction through kernel ridge regression (KRR), finding that KRR on the learned feature kernel yields scalar inflation of the KRR estimator at initialization -- an "anti-shrinkage" mechanism that reinflates task-relevant directions suppressed by ridge, while also amplifying noise. To study when this inflation improves generalization, in the overparameterized proportional limit we derive closed-form expressions for the bias, variance, and generalization errors of these estimators in terms of key macroscopic parameters -- notably the spike strength and spike-target alignment. Crucially, we find that a one-step generalization advantage vanishes for isotropic inputs and appears when both the spike strength and an effective signal-to-noise ratio are sufficiently large, demonstrating that a successful first gradient step both requires and benefits from low-dimensional task structure.

title: An $Ω(T^{3/4})$ lower bound for projection-free online learning with linear minimization oracles
summary:
This work considers projection-free online learning algorithms with linear minimization oracles for handling the decision set. For Online Frank--Wolfe (OFW), regret upper bounds were already known for specific OFW tunings [Hazan and Kale, 2012, Hazan, 2016] which scaled as $T^{3/4}$ (where $T$ is the horizon length). However, it remained an open question whether the regret of all OFW tunings scaled as $T^{3/4}$.
  We answer that question, proving a universal worst-case regret lower bound $Ω(T^{3/4} m^{-1/4})$ for any projection-free algorithm that makes at most $m$ linear minimization oracle calls per round. The analysis suggests an extended OFW to resort to multiple linear optimizations per round, for which we prove a regret upper bound $O(\max \{ T^{3/4} m^{-1/4}, \sqrt{T} \})$.

title: Finite-Sample Optimal Conformal Prediction Sets under Covariate Shift
summary:
We study conformal prediction under covariate shift with a known covariate density ratio, seeking prediction sets with minimum expected length under the target distribution. For every calibration sample size, we prove that the rule combining the inverse conditional-density score with randomized weighted conformal calibration minimizes this expected length among all rules valid over the full weighted-exchangeability class.
  We approximate the oracle using quantile and kernel histograms, including forest-weighted estimators, and select estimators and tuning parameters by resampling to estimate calibrated target length. On a bounded response domain, we bound excess length linearly in $L^1$ density error at fixed calibration size, without requiring a uniform positive lower bound on the true density. We also bound selection-pool and resampling errors. Under explicit growth conditions, the selected procedure approaches the same oracle while the calibration size remains fixed.
  Experiments on 36 known-density configurations and four public regression datasets compare coverage, prediction-set length, and runtime with existing methods.
  In targeted low-coverage and strong-shift comparisons, inverse-density selection yields shorter mean sets in most cases and lower mean runtime than the evaluated weighted baselines, with some differences in achieved coverage.

title: New Multiple Descent Phenomena Induced by Heterogeneous Data
summary: Modern machine learning models are often trained on large datasets assembled from many different sources, whose statistical properties can differ substantially. Understanding how this heterogeneity affects generalization performance is therefore important for explaining how model performance changes as model size increases. In this work, we study this question in linear random-feature models and show that mixtures of datasets with different covariance structures can give rise to a range of multiple-descent phenomena. We derive exact asymptotic expressions for the test error of each data source in the high-dimensional regime, and show how heterogeneity in covariance scale and spectral structure can introduce additional, group-dependent interpolation thresholds as model size increases. These phenomena arise even with noiseless labels and linear activations, showing that neither label noise nor activation nonlinearity is necessary for multiple-descent. Our results therefore provide a different perspective from classical explanations of multiple descent. More broadly, our results have potential implications for algorithmic fairness by showing that model scaling can affect different data groups unevenly, amplifying disparities in their generalization errors. We validate our theoretical results on synthetic Gaussian mixtures and real-world datasets, including MNIST and CIFAR-10.

title: Wasserstein Bounds for Euler and Randomized Midpoint Langevin Sampling with Noisy Gradients
summary: Stochastic-gradient Langevin methods are sampling algorithms that replace the gradient of the log probability density by a noisy, possibly biased evaluation. We study how such gradient-evaluation errors affect the Euler and randomized midpoint discretizations of Langevin dynamics by comparing each noisy chain with its exact-gradient counterpart. For continuously differentiable, strongly log-concave targets with globally Lipschitz gradients, we derive comparison bounds under a sub-Gaussian condition on the gradient noise. The resulting 2-Wasserstein bounds hold uniformly over iterations, and are linear in both the step size and the $L^2$ norm of the evaluation bias, with a square-root dependence on dimensionality. To the best of our knowledge, no comparable 2-Wasserstein bounds have previously been established for randomized midpoint with noisy gradients. For Euler, our results complement recent Wasserstein bounds by allowing biased evaluations, and by not requiring additional regularity assumptions on the evaluation errors.

title: Combining Multiple Incomplete Astronomical Surveys to Estimate Galaxy Flux Distributions
comment: 35 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: In astrophysics, the distributions of fluxes or intensities of populations of sources provide insight into the structure and evolution of the universe. We propose a science-driven hierarchical Bayesian framework to estimate the X-ray flux distribution of a population of galaxies. The distribution is parameterized via a broken power law model, formulated as a mixture of Pareto distributions, and is fit using data from a combination of non-representative X-ray and optical surveys. Because fainter sources are less likely to be detected, astronomical surveys suffer from incompleteness at the low-intensity end, and dedicated survey simulations are used to study the resulting missing-data pattern and determine the form of corrections. We introduce a methodology to combine data from two (or more) surveys with different incompleteness functions. This allows us to leverage deeper surveys (e.g., optical) to more fully characterize the X-ray log(N)-log(S) (where fewer sources are detected). We take advantage of a well-calibrated characterization of the missing-data pattern, particularly in X-ray surveys, to make incompleteness corrections for sources that are not detected in either survey. The proposed model is validated using a simulation study designed to mimic the Chandra Deep Field South (CDF-S), demonstrating accurate recovery of the flux distribution even under high proportions of systematic incompleteness. Finally, we apply our proposed method to data from the CDF-S.

title: Model Criticism via Stochastic Optimization
summary: Many generative models are specified by how data are simulated. An observation is a deterministic transform $Y=G(θ,X)$ of a draw $X$ from an assumed noise law, indexed by a structural parameter $θ$. Such models cover discrete, continuous and functional data, as well as i.i.d. replicates of stochastic processes, but their likelihoods are often unavailable. We propose a simulation-based procedure that tests whether such a model fits the data and, when it does not, locates where it fails, without choosing a test statistic. The procedure splits the data in two and is formulated as a two-stage stochastic program. In the estimation stage, $θ$ is fitted on the first block by minimizing a Wasserstein distance between the data and simulations from the model. In the recourse stage, $θ$ is frozen at the fitted $\tildeθ$, and a finite set of representative noise values $\{\bar x_j\}$ is pushed through the fitted mechanism to give model atoms $G(\tildeθ,\bar x_j)$. The held-out block optimizes weights $\textbf{w}$ on the model atoms to best match its own distribution. The optimized weights are then compared with theoretical weights under correct specification. Since each model atom is the image of known noise values, the disagreement between optimal and theoretical weights points to the part of the noise law that is wrong. The split makes the scaled weights conditionally multinomial, yielding a calibrated Pearson test. We prove strong consistency of both stages under checkable assumptions and illustrate the procedure on a Gaussian location--scale family, the number of segregating sites under Kingman's coalescent, a Yule process, and an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck diffusion.

title: fastC-GC and fastC-GC*: Efficient RCCP-Guided Graph Estimation for Time Series
summary: We introduce fastC-GC and fastC-GC$^*$, computationally efficient methods for time-series graph estimation using the two-test rule motivated by Reichenbach's common cause principle (RCCP) and the conditioning sets of causalised Granger causality (c-GC and c-GC$^*$). The methods use standardized data, ridge-residual correlation, and complete circular shift enumeration evaluated by Fourier transforms. Shared precision calculations and Schur downdates avoid repeated regression fits. On a single-threaded benchmark, fastC-GC was 68-277 times faster than the compared c-GC implementation, and fastC-GC$^*$ was 192-886 times faster than c-GC$^*$. Across four suites with reference graphs, aggregate mean area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) differed from the corresponding baseline by at most 0.019, but F1 was lower at the selected thresholds in every suite. The computational gains therefore accompany a change in estimator and selected graphs. Among eight methods, Bagged PCMCI+ had the highest mean AUPRC on sparse VAR, an autocorrelated structural process, and DREAM3; CUTS+ led on Lorenz-96. Wind-tunnel and river-discharge applications illustrate differences between inferred graphs without establishing causal accuracy. We prove the computational identities and a restricted population adjacency result for fastC-GC$^*$. Causal interpretation requires the stated graphical assumptions; validity of the implemented tests additionally requires a suitable shift-invariant null law. Empirical null rejection rates informed the conditional threshold $β= 0.005$, without establishing general test validity or graph-wide error control.

title: What's Old Is New: Improved Learning from Small-Group Tutorials
comment: 16 pages, 2 tables. Code and synthetic data: https://github.com/dlsun/tutorials
summary: The ubiquity of Large Language Models poses a challenge to student learning in homework-based college courses, where access to easy homework answers devalues the intended productive struggle. To address this concern, we propose Oxbridge-style weekly tutorials, where students present homework problems without notes in a small group with an instructor or TA. We conducted a randomized experiment in an introductory probability class to evaluate the effectiveness of tutorials, finding a significant positive effect of tutorial enrollment on exam grades. We discuss the implementation, challenges, and opportunities in this style of course design.

title: Efficient Deep Gaussian Process Surrogates via Mini-Batch Latent MAP Estimation
comment: 35 pages including references, 11 pages appendix, 5 figures
summary: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are flexible surrogate models for computer experiments with nonstationary response surfaces, but inference over their latent representations remains computationally challenging. Existing methods typically rely on variational inference or Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which impose variational-family assumptions or require costly posterior sampling. We propose the latent maximum-a-posteriori deep Gaussian process (LaMP-DGP), which uses gradient-based optimization to obtain MAP estimates of the latent representations and enables efficient probabilistic prediction through linked-GP calculations. To scale LaMP-DGP to large datasets, we develop a mini-batch optimization algorithm and, under a polynomial mini-batch bias-decay condition, establish a stationarity bound for latent-state optimization that motivates a growing batch-size schedule. Across numerical experiments and real-data analyses, LaMP-DGP provides consistently competitive predictive performance relative to doubly stochastic variational inference, stochastic gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and fully Bayesian Vecchia DGP inference. Computationally, LaMP-DGP is substantially faster than the Vecchia MCMC approach while remaining broadly competitive with the stochastic-gradient alternatives. These results position LaMP-DGP as a competitive and computationally efficient alternative for DGP inference. An R package, "LaMPDGP", is available for implementing the proposed method.

title: Scalable Bayesian Quadrature via Operator-Adapted Features
summary: Kernel methods face two recurrent bottlenecks: the cubic cost of inverting an $n\times n$ kernel matrix, as in kernel ridge regression, and the evaluation of kernel integrals, as required in kernel quadrature. Existing low-rank kernel and Gaussian process approximations primarily address the former bottleneck, but do not control the downstream quadrature error when both the kernel matrix and kernel mean are approximated, particularly when the integrand lies outside the kernel reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We address both challenges through an operator-adapted finite-feature approximation. Specifically, we construct a finite-dimensional working kernel from the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of a second-order differential operator. We establish convergence guarantees for the resulting finite-feature estimators in kernel quadrature, with extension to other related kernel methods. Our results show that, with $m \lesssim n$ basis functions, the truncated estimator attains the corresponding benchmark statistical rates. The theory covers fixed/random designs, noisy/noiseless observations, oversmoothing/undersmoothing regimes, and Matérn/Gaussian-type weights. We provide explicit error bounds that quantify the roles of the spectral cutoff, regularization parameter, lengthscale, sampling geometry, and operator boundary condition. We verify the convergence results in numerical experiments.

title: Opening Rankings from Engine Self-Play Are Less Certain Than They Look: Sampling Error, Draws, and Strength Dependence in Strength-Limited Stockfish Games
comment: 50 pages, including supplementary material. 6 main figures, 5 main tables. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23357406
summary: Engine self-play allows chess openings to be compared under controlled conditions, without the selection effects of human game databases. When openings differ only slightly, however, rankings built from a few hundred games can be unstable. In Study 1, strength-limited Stockfish 15.1 played 17,400 games: ten forced White first moves and ten forced Black replies to 1.e4, each at three strength settings. The leading opening changed between settings, twice by a single game. There was no statistically reliable evidence, though, that differences among openings depended on strength (White p = .311, Black p = .843). The design had limited sensitivity to isolated strength-dependent effects: a 12-point effect was detected by the omnibus test in only about 39% of simulated studies. A Connect Four positive control detected an observed 22.5-point center-column advantage, demonstrating sensitivity to large opening differences. With 290 games per opening, the observed leader was the true best of ten openings in only about 44% of simulated studies assuming a between-opening standard deviation of three percentage points. Follow-up studies with complete game records showed that the settings were ordered in direct matches but did not form a consistent Elo scale, that win and draw rates differed across hardware and implementation configurations, and that an apparent 1.d3 weakness was not confirmed in new games. With Stockfish 19 and a fixed node budget, survey-selected replies showed no statistically reliable advantage over free engine choice. Opening leaderboards from a few hundred engine games can overstate certainty.

title: Interpretable and Validatable Uplift Modeling
summary: Uplift models estimate treatment effects for individuals, but we do not observe individual treatment effects, so the predictions are hard to interpret and validate. A decision-maker often wants trustworthy claims about groups where the treatment is beneficial or harmful, and to know when a treatment benefits some people more than others. Our procedure provides such a set of claims, certified simultaneously at a specified familywise error rate (FWER). We summarize an uplift model by a shallow tree fit to its predictions. Each node of the tree carries two hypotheses, one about the average treatment effect in the node and one about the difference in effects across the node's split; the two kinds are interwoven into a single hierarchy. Splitting the data enables honest estimation in the evaluation set. It lets us choose the direction of each one-sided test from the training half, allowing us to certify the sign of treatment effects in subpopulations, and to compare effects between groups. We demonstrate our procedure offers strong control of the FWER.

title: Metropolized backward sampling for conditional sequential Monte Carlo
comment: 12 pages + appendix. A Lean formalization was AI-generated after the draft of the paper was written as an experiment. I have subsequently edited the documentation of the formalization for better readability, and discussed the process, as well as difference between the AI-formalized and my original proofs in the appendix. https://adriencorenflos.github.io/formalization/metropolized-CSMC/
summary: Particle Gibbs samplers with backward sampling are widely used for sampling the smoothing distribution of state-space models, but, with few particles, the new trajectory often coincides with the current one at many time steps. A known but rarely used remedy replaces the random selection of the final particle by a Metropolis--Hastings move which avoids the current particle. We show that, with backward sampling, this remedy only helps at the last time steps, because its effect on the update rates decays geometrically with the distance to the final time. We propose instead Metropolized backward sampling, which makes such a move at every step of the backward pass, forcibly switching trajectories whenever possible. Additionally, we introduce a coupled version which prevents proposing the current trajectory, maximizing the chances of an actual switch versus the current trajectory and performing perfect sampling when the state-space model has no observations, a feature not shared by backward sampling. We prove that, at every time step, both methods dominate backward sampling as they update the state more often and have smaller lag-one autocorrelations than it does. Our methods are drop-in replacements for backward sampling, and can be used to improve any particle Gibbs sampler.

title: Interpretable Feature Discovery from Unstructured Data Using LLMs and Statistical Choice Models
summary: Feature extraction from unstructured data typically relies on opaque embeddings unsuited to interpretable decision-making. Interpretable features, on the other hand, typically require costly, and often infeasible, hand-engineering. Large language models (LLMs) offer a natural bridge, as they can read raw data and describe it in interpretable terms. One could simply ask an LLM to extract features from a large sample of the dataset, but context limitations and diluted attention can lead to unsatisfactory results. We introduce a method that automatically discovers interpretable, decision-relevant features from unstructured data. Our key idea is to perform pairwise comparisons between items, asking an LLM to articulate, in interpretable terms, the features distinguishing each pair. We treat these explanations, or rationales, as data: we develop a statistical choice model that combines these rationales across the comparisons to identify relevant features and estimate per-item, per-feature scores. We first test our method on a synthetic hiring dataset of cover letters with known ground-truth features and show that it significantly outperforms direct LLM feature extraction in feature recovery. We then apply it to the ChangeMyView (Reddit) debate dataset, where it discovers several interpretable features associated with persuasion while reaching predictive accuracy comparable to established baselines. We also show how the same rationales can be used to audit LLM decisions, yielding a holistic score whose decomposition over interpretable features reveals what the LLM rewards.

title: High-dimensional two-sample testing: From optimal transport to optimal derangements
summary: In recent years, optimal transport has emerged as a useful framework for constructing distribution-free multivariate two-sample tests by transporting observations to a reference distribution under a suitable transportation cost. However, existing optimal transport-based tests can perform poorly in high dimension, low sample size (HDLSS) settings, and their performance depends critically on the choice of the reference distribution and transportation cost. We investigate this phenomenon and show that suitable choices can substantially improve their performance. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce a class of two-sample tests based on optimal derangements that do not require an external reference distribution. The minimum distance pairing test of Rosenbaum arises as a special case when the optimization is restricted to a subclass of derangements, thereby revealing a connection between this method and optimal transport. We propose the optimal derangement (ODER) test and its distribution-free variant, the ODER-SHC test, obtained by restricting the minimization to derangements consisting of a single Hamiltonian cycle. We establish their consistency under both HDLSS and classical large-sample asymptotic regimes. We also develop corresponding procedures based on the $L1$ distance and establish their high-dimensional consistency under conditions involving coordinate-wise energy distances. These $L1$ distance based tests can also discriminate between two high-dimensional distributions with identical first two moments but different marginal distributions. Analyses of benchmark datasets and extensive simulation studies demonstrate the performance of the proposed methods across a variety of alternatives and data settings.

title: A simple sensitivity analysis for observational studies
summary: Drawing causal conclusions from non-experimental (observational) data is a central aim in science but is extremely challenging. Without control over treatment assignment (as in an experiment), treated and control groups may not be comparable on unmeasured factors affecting treatment and outcome. To address such concerns, sensitivity analyses can be performed; sensitivity analyses acknowledge the existence of unmeasured factors but ask how strong they must be to overturn causal conclusions. We (re)introduce a particularly simple form of sensitivity analysis which can be performed by any reader of an observational study with access to only an estimate and confidence interval for a causal effect. This simple sensitivity analysis may serve as an effective tool for readers wishing to gauge the robustness of conclusions from an observational study.

title: L-PASSO: Adaptive Log-penalized Variable Selector, with Sparse Selection and Robustness to the Pilot Estimator
summary: We study L-PASSO, a penalized least-squares regression method based on the logarithmic penalty $λ\sum_j\log(1+|β_j|/τ)$, and its two-stage adaptive form, in which the scales $τ_j$ come from a pilot estimator. Although this concave penalty has been proposed previously, its variable-selection properties and sparsity relative to other popular penalties have not been fully characterized. We derive the exact orthogonal-design solution, and show that the single-stage estimator selects the true model under a weighted irrepresentable condition that holds for every design once $τ$ is small. We further establish that, under matched tuning, the two-stage estimator possesses the oracle property and has half the asymptotic bias of the adaptive LASSO. Our main theoretical contribution concerns the robustness of the two-stage procedure to the pilot estimator. We show that two-stage L-PASSO remains selection consistent even when the weights associated with relevant variables are as small as $\exp\{-o(1/ζ_n)\}$, whereas the adaptive LASSO fails to retain relevant variables whose pilot weights are sufficiently small relative to its tuning parameter $ζ_n$. We establish that both thresholds are sharp. In high-dimensional settings, we prove support recovery for a local minimizer without imposing any lower-bound condition on the weights of relevant variables, and provide conditions under which this local minimizer is also the unique global minimizer. We additionally establish the selection consistency of a BIC-based tuning-parameter selection procedure. Finally, simulations comparing L-PASSO with the LASSO, SCAD, MCP, SELO, uniLasso, and the adaptive LASSO show that L-PASSO most frequently recovers the true support. Two real-data examples further illustrate the method.

title: Sequince: a modular sequential Monte Carlo toolkit
comment: 7 pages. Describes sequince v0.1.0, available on PyPI. Code: https://github.com/sequince-dev/sequince. Documentation: https://sequince.readthedocs.io/. PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/sequince/
summary: Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods approximate sequences of probability distributions using populations of weighted samples and are widely applicable, including in Bayesian inference and particle filtering. We present sequince, a modular Python toolkit for constructing SMC algorithms from reusable and extensible components. The toolkit provides modular steps for weighting, resampling, mutation, transformation, and control operations that are composed to implement different algorithms. It also includes prebuilt samplers for tempered SMC, persistent sampling and nested sampling via SMC. Its core components follow the Python Array API standard, supporting NumPy, JAX, PyTorch, and CuPy, enabling analyses on CPUs or GPUs. Random-number control and checkpointing support reproducible scientific workflows. This paper describes sequince v0.1.0 and its design as reusable infrastructure for methodological research and application of SMC methods.

title: MiniMMD: Minimization of MMD for Sampling, Inference and Integration
summary: Many problems in computational statistics and machine learning can be formulated as approximating a target distribution by minimizing a discrepancy over a restricted class of candidate distributions. This minimum-discrepancy viewpoint appears, for example, in numerical integration, sampling, generative modelling, and statistical inference, but these instances are often studied separately in the literature. This thesis develops the first unified treatment of these many problems through the minimization of the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), a kernel-based discrepancy between probability measures. The central theme is that MMD is not only a statistically meaningful distance between probability distributions, but also a tractable optimization objective to design practical and efficient algorithms. This thesis summarizes the recent theoretical and empirical advancements of such minimum-MMD based algorithms.

title: Central limit theorems for high-dimensional ridge regression under uniform subsampling
summary: We study ridge regression based on uniformly subsampled observations in high-dimensional linear models, where the number of predictors and the sample size grow proportionally. Subsampling is implemented through independent Bernoulli indicators with a common selection probability. We establish central limit theorems for linear contrasts of the ridge estimator, allowing for non-Gaussian predictors and general population covariance matrices. Under a vanishing-signal assumption, we obtain an explicit bias correction in the isotropic case and develop consistent estimators of the asymptotic variances. These results enable asymptotically valid tests for linear contrasts of the regression parameter in the isotropic setting. Our proofs exploit the resolvent representation of the ridge estimator and combine leave-one-out arguments with deterministic equivalents from random matrix theory.

title: Length-Preserving Vessel Trajectory Simplification With Controllable Compression-Precision Bound
comment: accepted for publish in Ocean Engineering
summary: Vessel trajectory data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS) is important for a wide range of maritime analysis and management applications. As AIS datasets continue to grow in scale, trajectory simplification (or compression) algorithms have become indispensable tools for managing their computational demands. Existing approaches, however, largely overlook the preservation of trajectory length, a critical metric of direct relevance to maritime environmental auditing and voyage management. We address this gap by framing trajectory simplification as a pair of dual optimization problems subject to error constraints: Compression-Driven Simplification (CDS), which minimizes data volume for a given length-error tolerance, and Precision-Driven Simplification (PDS), which minimizes length approximation error for a given compression target. Both problems are solved within a unified dynamic programming framework, and we provide mathematical proofs establishing that our formulation yields globally optimal solutions. This guarantees flexible, direct control over both compression ratio and length-approximation fidelity. { We benchmark CDS and PDS on real-world AIS datasets spanning diverse navigation scenarios and representative water area, comparing against state-of-the-art baselines. Experimental results on public benchmark datasets demonstrate that even under a small length error tolerance ($ε=0.1$ nmi), our methods achieve about 91\% data compression rate, approximately 14\% higher than the best-performing baseline, which implies that our methods are capable of maximally preserving the trajectory length while reducing data redundancy significant.

title: Weighting Scheme and Construction in IPCW Survival Estimation
summary:
Inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW) is widely used to address dependent censoring in survival analysis. Beyond estimation of the censoring distribution, its implementation requires specifying how inverse probability weights are incorporated into survival estimators. IPCW does not uniquely determine this construction, and different choices can produce different finite-sample behavior even under the same censoring model.
  In this work, we examine a class of IPCW estimators for the survival function, distinguishing hazard-based from margin-based formulations and time-varying from fixed weighting schemes. We show how these choices affect structural validity, stability, and finite-sample performance. In particular, the weight-changing hazard (WCH) estimator applies time-varying censoring weights within a product-limit construction with risk-set normalization, ensuring monotonicity and boundedness when the weighted risk-set denominators are positive. Through simulation studies under varying levels of covariate-dependent and administrative censoring, we demonstrate that WCH achieves favorable bias--variance tradeoffs and improved finite-sample stability relative to the alternative IPCW constructions examined, particularly in settings with few observed events or heavy censoring. We further illustrate these differences using data from the Women's Interagency HIV Study (WIHS), in which alternative IPCW constructions produced meaningfully different survival curves.
  Overall, our findings emphasize that the effectiveness of IPCW depends on both the weighting scheme and the estimator formulation. Careful consideration of these choices is therefore important for reliable survival estimation under dependent censoring.

title: Reframing Spatial Uncertainty Visualisation with a Layered Grammar of Graphics
summary: Communicating both estimated values and their associated uncertainties presents a particular challenge in spatial visualisation because spatial coordinates already occupy the primary visual channels, leaving relatively few channels available for encoding uncertainty alongside the estimated values. A range of visualisation techniques has been developed to address this challenge, including bivariate choropleth maps, pixel maps, and glyph maps. However, existing implementations typically treat these techniques as dedicated visualisations rather than expressing them through the composable elements of a grammar of graphics. We reframe uncertainty visualisation as an extension of the layered grammar of graphics, allowing uncertainty-specific representations to be composed, customised, and extended alongside other graphical components. We demonstrate this perspective by integrating uncertainty visualisation into the layered architecture of ggplot2, accommodating these techniques while also motivating new approaches such as the dual map for selective attention between estimated values and their associated uncertainties. We implement the framework in the R package ggincerta and demonstrate its application through three case studies.

title: Capacity of the Hopfield-Hebbian dynamics with correlated patterns
summary:
Allowing for small fraction of errors in retrieved stored binary patterns, Hopfield-Hebbian neural network (NN) associative memory dynamics [14] achieves linearly scaled capacity. The famous proportionality constant $α_c\approx 0.14$ is obtained in a large dimensional scenario as the ratio of the number of reliably stored patterns $m$ and the patterns' length $n$ under the assumption that uniformly randomly chosen binary patterns are \emph{independent} among themselves.
  While such an idealized scenario is now well understood, more practical scenarios with correlated/noisy datasets remaining challenging even for classical statistical mechanics replica approaches. We consider precisely such practical settings where each \emph{archetype} pattern is replaced with $M$ correlated \emph{examples} with parameter $r$ governing the quality of correlation. We develop a powerful Random Duality Theory (RDT) based framework to analyze correlated data and already on the first level of RDT lifting obtain capacity characterizations that remarkably well match behavior exhibited through simulated dynamics. Moreover, characterizations explicitly feature correlation parameters $M$ and $r$, which allows to precisely determine their effects on phase-transitioning behavior of the underlying dynamics.
  Our results are also a well-fitting complement to the existing literature. Namely, to circumvent challenging statistical mechanics analyses, an alternative combination of spectral and replica methods is considered in [4]. We confirm that [4]'s elegant spectral characterizations are excellent approximations in the low correlated regime. At the same time, we also close the gap in the regimes with higher correlation levels where spectral methods deviate from the practical dynamics performance.

title: Order invariance of the generalized Rosenblatt transform on standard Borel spaces
summary: The Rosenblatt transform maps a random vector to independent uniform variables through successive conditional distribution functions; for laws on $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with atomless conditional distributions and a fixed order of the coordinates, it is the almost surely unique monotone triangular map with this property. For a fixed reference law, transform-based tests remain valid under every fixed admissible order, but that choice can still affect their statistical power. For fixed orders, we establish identification and uniqueness results for this extended generalized Rosenblatt transform (EGRT) that parallel those for the classical transform. We then characterize order dependence in two senses: first demonstrating conditions under which the EGRT is invariant under linear extensions of prescribed partial orders, and second showing that under every admissible order the output of the EGRT retains all the statistical information from the input observations over reference-dominated families. We close with a brief discussion of what these results mean for the relationship between order choice and goodness-of-fit testing.

title: Statistical Elements of a Successful Farm-scale Trial
summary: Growers and advisers increasingly run large strip trials on their own paddocks, but the rules used to design them come from small-plot research. We simulated strip trials on a spatially autocorrelated field, varying trial length (L), replication (r), randomised or systematic allocation, and long-strip or stacked layout, for a nitrogen response that was uniform or varied across within-field pseudo-environments (PEs). Analyses of strip-plot means and of yield pixels were first checked for Type I error, and designs were then compared by the smallest response that a valid analysis detects with 80% power. Follow-up runs added gaps, unequal strip lengths, trends, spatially varying responses and alternative field structures; more than 3 million models were fitted. Treating pixels as independent replicates gave false positives in 32-40% of null trials. Replication was the strongest design lever: the detectable response scaled as $r^{-0.60}$ to $r^{-1.02}$ but only as $L^{-0.45}$ or more slowly, and at equal plot area more, shorter replicates won all 66 comparisons. With complete data, strip means with an autoregressive residual were the most precise analysis; when strips contained gaps, pixel-level spatial models with a strip effect halved the detectable response, while the spatial analysis of strip means became liberal. For PE-varying responses, spatial PE models detected per-PE effects 33-46% smaller than PE means without a spatial term. Randomisation did not improve precision but kept tests valid (systematic allocation: Type I error up to 23%), whereas systematic allocation gave more accurate response maps. The results are condensed into a design table and a detectable-gain chart for use before a trial is sown.

title: Combining Adaptive Seamless Phase II/III Designs and Group Sequential Analysis for Time-to-Event Endpoints in Oncology Trials
summary: Seamless Phase II/III designs are a natural vehicle for the randomized dose optimization called for by the US Food and Drug Administration's Project Optimus initiative. Their extension to group sequential repeated testing of a time-to-event endpoint after end-of-Phase-II dose selection, however, remains largely unestablished. Existing proposals index the boundaries for the post-selection looks by the overall information fraction of the primary endpoint---the correct index for the log-rank statistics of an unadapted trial, but not for the combination statistics these designs actually test---and support family-wise error rate (FWER) control by simulation. We instead work from the joint distribution of the combination statistics themselves, calibrating group sequential boundaries separately for each hypothesis in the closure and applying closed testing at every look; a general lemma establishes that this controls the FWER in the strong sense, for any number of hypotheses and analysis times. Specifically, under patient-wise separation and an inverse-normal combination test, the interim and final statistics for an individual hypothesis are bivariate normal, with a correlation determined by how the events at each look divide between the pre- and post-selection cohorts rather than by the overall information fraction, so that their boundaries follow from standard group sequential software; the corresponding statistics for the intersection hypothesis, formed from a Hochberg-adjusted Stage-1 $p$-value, are not multivariate normal, and we obtain their boundaries by a dedicated numerical integration. Head-to-head against a recently proposed incremental-Dunnett procedure, the two were near-identical when the design projections were correct, but ours was more robust when the combination weights were based on a misprojected division of the Stage~1 events either side of the interim.

title: Model Criticism via Stochastic Optimization
summary: Many generative models are specified by how data are simulated. An observation is a deterministic transform $Y=G(θ,X)$ of a draw $X$ from an assumed noise law, indexed by a structural parameter $θ$. Such models cover discrete, continuous and functional data, as well as i.i.d. replicates of stochastic processes, but their likelihoods are often unavailable. We propose a simulation-based procedure that tests whether such a model fits the data and, when it does not, locates where it fails, without choosing a test statistic. The procedure splits the data in two and is formulated as a two-stage stochastic program. In the estimation stage, $θ$ is fitted on the first block by minimizing a Wasserstein distance between the data and simulations from the model. In the recourse stage, $θ$ is frozen at the fitted $\tildeθ$, and a finite set of representative noise values $\{\bar x_j\}$ is pushed through the fitted mechanism to give model atoms $G(\tildeθ,\bar x_j)$. The held-out block optimizes weights $\textbf{w}$ on the model atoms to best match its own distribution. The optimized weights are then compared with theoretical weights under correct specification. Since each model atom is the image of known noise values, the disagreement between optimal and theoretical weights points to the part of the noise law that is wrong. The split makes the scaled weights conditionally multinomial, yielding a calibrated Pearson test. We prove strong consistency of both stages under checkable assumptions and illustrate the procedure on a Gaussian location--scale family, the number of segregating sites under Kingman's coalescent, a Yule process, and an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck diffusion.

title: A goodness of fit approach to select the optimal visit sequence for nonparametric data synthesis
summary: Synthetic data are a promising way to maintain privacy while disseminating research data, thereby enabling compliance with the open science principles. Popular methods for generating synthetic data include sequential synthesis, where each variable is generated conditionally on the preceding ones in a given order. This order, also called the visit sequence of the synthesizer, is known to affect the quality of synthetic data. This raises the question of the criteria that should guide its choice. In this work, we present a novel method to perform such selection based on a goodness of fit criterion, and show that it outperforms alternative structure-based methods, both in terms of synthesis quality and time complexity. The proposed method also has the advantage of being applicable to any type of data and any class of conditional distribution models.

title: Noise Calibration and Exact Recovery for Multiview Ordinal Rearrangement Data
summary: We studied simultaneous recovery of a latent group count, subject partition, and signature means from multiview ordinal ranks. A normalized reference rearrangement score is an affine Spearman correlation; the problem concerns the information retained by several such scores and their noise geometry. We develop an ordered-gap estimator with direction-specific concentration radii. Its finite-sample guarantee separates signature noise, missing groups, and candidate coverage, and allows the group count to grow under an attainable-margin condition. A coordinatewise partition followed by label-tuple refinement recovers groups even when every individual coordinate has population collisions. A binary-code construction explains why the one-dimensional inverse-group margin restriction need not govern a retained coordinate bank. We derive actual-law concentration from bounded ranking modules and a fixed-dimensional combinatorial central limit theorem under an observed permutation representation. A binary ordinal submodel gives logarithmic exact-recovery information scales. A subject-effect construction distinguishes persistent overlap from reducible measurement noise, and an additional ordinal anchor quantifies how new information lowers that error floor. Five focused simulation scenarios illustrate direction-specific calibration, growing-group recovery, coordinate collision resolution, variance reduction, and the effect of an additional ordinal anchor.

title: Compartment-driven Gaussian processes for uncertainty quantification of pharmacokinetic exposures
summary: Pharmacokinetic modeling is a crucial part of drug development. An important goal is to estimate patients' total and peak exposure to a drug over time, quantified by the area under the concentration--time curve (AUC) and the maximum concentration ($C_{\max}$) respectively. Such exposure assessment is essential to balance efficacy and safety in medications that offer therapeutic benefits but carry risks of toxicity, such as chemotherapy drugs. Uncertainty quantification for exposure quantities, however, remains challenging, since they are functionals of an often sparsely observed concentration--time curve with measurement errors. We propose a compartment-driven Gaussian process framework that propagates uncertainty in concentration--time curves to pharmacokinetic exposure functionals. Our approach uses pharmacokinetic compartmental models to specify a mechanistically informed prior and Gaussian processes to accommodate departures from the assumed pharmacokinetic dynamics. The framework can accommodate both individual-level and group-aggregated concentration--time data commonly seen in practice. We provide straightforward computational procedures for drawing posterior inference on AUC and $C_{\max}$. Simulations across a range of observation schemes demonstrate robustness to departures from the assumed compartmental dynamics. We apply the method to patient-level datasets on warfarin and theophylline, and aggregated data from a chemotherapy study of 5-fluorouracil and capecitabine in patients with normal or impaired hepatic function. The chemotherapy analysis quantifies drug-specific exposure differences between groups with differing liver function, with potential implications for informing dosing decisions.

title: Robust Global Testing for Mean Functions in Sparse and Dense Functional and Longitudinal Data
summary: We develop a robust quadratic score test for a specified mean function in functional and longitudinal data. The construction combines a convex loss with subject-level scores while retaining dependence among repeated measurements. An explicit score-centering condition ensures that the target remains the population mean. We establish the null distribution and Sobolev separation rates under sparse and dense sampling, identifying a transition from a nonparametric testing rate to the root-n boundary. A Gaussian multiplier bootstrap remains valid across these regimes, including settings with non-Gaussian quadratic limits. For implementation, we use a finite spline approximation and estimate the curvature through symmetric score increments. Under the stated conditions, the feasible procedure preserves null calibration and attains a consistency separation rate matching the lower bound over model classes containing a Gaussian submodel. Simulations illustrate the performance of squared, Huber, and absolute losses under regular errors and contamination, and an analysis of longitudinal CD4 counts demonstrates the method.

title: Wasserstein Bounds for Euler and Randomized Midpoint Langevin Sampling with Noisy Gradients
summary: Stochastic-gradient Langevin methods are sampling algorithms that replace the gradient of the log probability density by a noisy, possibly biased evaluation. We study how such gradient-evaluation errors affect the Euler and randomized midpoint discretizations of Langevin dynamics by comparing each noisy chain with its exact-gradient counterpart. For continuously differentiable, strongly log-concave targets with globally Lipschitz gradients, we derive comparison bounds under a sub-Gaussian condition on the gradient noise. The resulting 2-Wasserstein bounds hold uniformly over iterations, and are linear in both the step size and the $L^2$ norm of the evaluation bias, with a square-root dependence on dimensionality. To the best of our knowledge, no comparable 2-Wasserstein bounds have previously been established for randomized midpoint with noisy gradients. For Euler, our results complement recent Wasserstein bounds by allowing biased evaluations, and by not requiring additional regularity assumptions on the evaluation errors.

title: Pinpointing Pivot Points: The DECIDE Framework for Data Analysis Decision Importances
summary: Human judgment calls made throughout the data science life cycle can change the conclusions drawn from data. Independent analysts often make different choices when given the same data, leading to often unacceptable variations in results and contributing to the ongoing reproducibility crisis across scientific disciplines. The rapid adoption of agentic tools threatens to amplify this crisis. Several approaches have been developed to address this variation by following the same strategy: repeating an analysis under different combinations of analytical decisions and inspecting the distribution of outcomes. Examples include multiverse analysis, specification curve analysis, and vibration of effects. More broadly, the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) framework assesses how documented judgment calls across the data science life cycle affect conclusions, with predictability serving as a reality-check that a model captures signal. Each of these approaches results in a "multiverse" object. While the distribution of outcomes reflects the overall variability of conclusions, estimating the influence of each individual decision requires additional tools. A common heuristic is to train a model to predict the outcome from these decisions and treat its coefficients or feature importances as proxies for each decision's influence. Although this strategy may work in certain cases, it assumes the model is correctly specified and accurately predicts the outcome, which we show is not always the case. In this work, we introduce DECIDE, a model-free framework that quantifies each decision's importance from the actual outcomes across the plausible decision space, avoiding issues of predictability by design. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DECIDE by applying it to real-world multiverse analyses. We further provide what is, to our knowledge, the first formal definition of the multiverse.

title: A Spectral Boundary for Independence Learnability
summary: Learning independence is fundamental to statistical inference and machine learning, yet learning independence between entire time series by a test remains challenging when only a single observation record is available. Existing guarantees often rely on structural or mixing assumptions, while stationarity and ergodicity alone do not permit consistent testing. In this work, we identify a class-level boundary governed by shared nontrivial Koopman eigenvalues, which represent common persistent oscillatory frequencies of the two processes. When no such eigenvalues are shared, we extend shift-based rank calibration with finite-window dependence witnesses and a data-adaptive threshold to construct a deterministic, weakly consistent test with finite-sample false-positive control, without quantitative mixing assumptions. Conversely, we show that no possibly randomized test can achieve vanishing false-positive probabilities under every independent jointly totally ergodic law while consistently detecting every dependent jointly totally ergodic law with a shared nontrivial eigenvalue. This impossibility already holds for binary observations and persists within any prescribed nonempty open eigenvalue window, identifying a spectral obstruction to universal learning of full-process independence.

title: Distributional Flexibility under Box-Cox Normality: A Theoretical and Empirical Evaluation of the Power-Normal Distribution
summary: Methods based on Box-Cox models have recently been developed for inference on clinically interpretable treatment effects in clinical trials. These methods model marginal outcome distributions using the power-normal distribution (PND), but the range of real-world data distributions that it can adequately approximate remains unclear. We evaluated PND approximations using two parameterizations of the four-parameter generalized $F$/generalized beta of the second kind family and 165 laboratory variables from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Overall distributional agreement was assessed using the overlap coefficient and Jensen-Shannon divergence, and location and spread on the original scale were evaluated using relative biases in the median and interquartile range. The PND closely approximated a broad range of smooth unimodal positive distributions in both the theoretical and empirical evaluations. Reduced agreement was associated with pronounced lower-bound accumulation, heaping or discretization, and multicomponent or peak-tail features. These features may be recognizable before fitting and provide practical guidance for assessing the suitability of the PND. We also developed the R package powerNormal for distributional calculations, parameter estimation, reparameterization, and random-number generation for the PND.

title: Integrating multi-source local information for global undirected graph reconstruction via integer programming
summary: Graphical models are widely used to represent conditional independence structures, but learning them is challenging when data are fragmented across sources that measure different subsets of variables and may not be directly shareable. We develop a general framework for reconstructing a shared global graph from heterogeneous, partially observed sources. Our framework permits both the observed variable sets and source-specific distributions to differ. Under a source-wise faithfulness condition, local conditional independence graphs correspond to latent projections of the shared global graph, which is identifiable up to the equivalence class induced by the observed variable sets. The framework integrates raw data, estimated source graphs, or a combination of both, accommodating settings with restricted access to individual-level data, such as privacy constraints. We develop mixed-integer optimization formulations and scalable approximate algorithms for several classes of graphical models. Unlike standard high-dimensional analyses, our guarantees are governed by new combinatorial notions of signal strength that capture how information propagates across partially observed sources. Extensive simulations further show that integration can substantially improve estimation of source-specific projected graphs relative to separate source methods. Real-data application illustrates the framework's use with partially-observed sources of fatty acid measurements.

title: Proximal R2 Priors for Structured Variance Allocation
summary: Scientific domain knowledge in regression often concerns structural relationships among model terms, which are typically encoded as parameter constraints. Since such relationships rarely hold exactly in practice, prior distributions should encourage them while at the same time retaining support for scientifically plausible departures. Accounting for these relationships becomes more pressing in modern regression, where high-dimensionality is usually present and regularisation is essential. $R^2$ decomposition priors provide an interpretable foundation for regularisation by placing a prior on total explained variance and distributing the implied signal across model terms. We introduce the Proximal R2 prior, which uses proximal relaxations to encode these relationships as soft constraints on the variance allocation. Our formulation yields differentiable posteriors compatible with standard gradient based samplers. Theoretically, we prove that our prior preserves the characteristic marginal properties of global-local shrinkage priors. Moreover, we establish posterior consistency and contraction rates in growing dimensions, showing that the inclusion of structural relationships and proximal methods do not alter the shrinkage properties. Notably, these results demonstrate that the structural constraints in the model do not hinder posterior recovery. Simulation studies and real-data applications to interaction and generalised additive models demonstrate that our prior improves parameter recovery, out-of-sample prediction, and sampling efficiency over existing constrained and unconstrained shrinkage priors, even under structural misspecification.

title: Memorization Capacity of Invariant Convolutional Neural Nets
summary: Neural networks are powerful memorizers which are often able to interpolate their training data even when the labels have been randomized. While there exists an extensive literature on the memorization capacity of fully connected networks, in practice more specific architectures with problem-dependent properties are preferred, such as convolutional networks for image classification. In this paper we consider convolutional networks which are invariant with respect to a given arbitrary finite group of orthogonal transformations, which may include translations, reflections, and/or rotations of images and invariances of higher order tensors. We prove upper bounds on the size of an invariant convolutional neural network with threshold activations that is required to interpolate a given dataset with two classes. Our bounds are formulated in terms of a complexity measure that takes the invariant structure into account and is instance-specific, i.e., it is related to the mutual arrangement of the classes in the given dataset and their geometric properties rather than the number of samples. Our proof is constructive: for given input data, instances of an interpolating network can be computed via a randomized algorithm with high probability. In numerical experiments we investigate the practical effectiveness of this algorithm.

summary: We study Bayesian estimation of conditional densities represented by normalized squares of orthogonal polynomial series. We specify the conditional density without modeling the marginal distribution of covariates. A prior on smoothness, the number of terms, and the coefficients gives adaptive posterior contraction at the minimax rate without a logarithmic factor when the normalized square-root representation of the true density is bounded away from zero and sufficiently smooth. For one outcome and $d_x$ covariates, the rate over classes with degree smoothness $s$ is $n^{-s/(2s+d_x+1)}$. The posterior predictive density attains the corresponding minimax squared Hellinger risk. For bounded nonnegative representations in Legendre and Chebyshev classes, we establish the minimax rate at every $s>0$. A prior that also permits a small mixture with the reference density adapts over these classes up to a logarithmic factor and retains the exact rate on the positive, sufficiently smooth subclass. Additional results concern identification, conditional distribution functions and quantiles, coefficient recovery and uniform convergence, independent Gaussian coefficient priors, and selection of polynomial terms.

title: Assessing the Role of Green Premium and Localized Price Spillovers in Budget Hotels : Evidence from Delhi National Capital Region (NCR)
summary: Sustainable urban tourism depends on how environmental quality, public transport accessibility, and accommo dation clustering shape visitor mobility and destination development. This study examines these relationships in the budget hotel sector of Delhi National Capital Region, India, an emerging mega-destination marked by rapid urban expansion and uneven infrastructure provision. Using data from 857 budget hotels, we estimate a mixed geographically weighted spatial autoregressive model that captures both spatial heterogeneity and localized price spillovers. The model combines hotel attributes with satellite- derived indicators, including vegetation density, built-up area, night-time light intensity, and distances to metro stations, bus stops, airports, city centers, and tourist attractions. Results show that greenery has a place-dependent value: it generates a green premium in dense urban cores, where environmental amenities are scarce, but becomes a discount in peripheral areas where vegetation often reflects weaker tourism infrastructure. Metro accessibility creates a mobility pre mium, highlighting the role of public transport in supporting low-cost tourist movement. Local spatial spillovers reveal agglomeration benefits in established clusters and price cannibalization in peripheral markets. The find ings show how spatially differentiated planning can align green infrastructure, transit investment, and budget accommodation with more sustainable urban tourism development.

title: Principal-agent hypothesis testing under adaptive experimentation
summary: Principal-agent hypothesis testing studies statistical contracts in which a principal rewards an agent according to data the agent generates. Existing work focuses on the single-shot setting, where the agent produces a single dataset. We extend the framework to sequential settings, where evidence accumulates over time, rewards may be deferred to the end or disbursed incrementally, and the agent may stop the contract at a strategically chosen stopping time. We call a contract null-deterring if no ''null agent'' (those whose data-generating distribution lies in the null hypothesis) can profit in expectation under any stopping rule, and our main conceptual result shows that such contracts are characterized by e-processes. We then turn to the agent's best response and identify the optimal stopping rule through the Snell envelope of the reward process. We develop simpler, more interpretable approximations that often require the agent to have only partial knowledge of its distribution.

title: Modular Bayesian Foundation Models: Bayesian time series encoders for OOD detection, routing and forecasting
summary: Industrial systems continuously generate time series that vary in sampling frequency, scale, dynamics, and operating regime. Consequently a single time-series foundation model may not be able to represent all regimes effectively and retraining a large model for every new dataset or regime shift is computationally expensive. Modular foundation models address this issue by reusing specialised encoders trained on diverse datasets and by allowing the expansion of capabilities through the addition of new experts. This approach requires compact experts to minimize storage cost and a proper selection mechanism of experts for unseen data. We propose a modular foundation model framework that combines end-to-end Bayesian encoder training with uncertainty based routing. Using Singular Bayesian Neural Networks (SBNNs), we build a collection of compact Bayesian encoders whose epistemic uncertainty guides label-free selection. At the selected ranks, our Bayesian collection uses 63.8\% less storage than its deterministic counterpart. We evaluate this framework on time-series data through distribution shift, encoder selection, and probabilistic forecasting. Across seven incoming datasets, uncertainty-based routing is competitive with distance-based routing in terms of forecast MSE, while reducing average ECE from 0.086 to 0.072 and average NLL from 0.907 to 0.836. It also increases PICP90 from 82.28\% to 89.03\%. In a separate model-family comparison, we evaluate the SBNN pipeline against full-rank Bayes by Backprop, deep ensembles, and MC Dropout. The SBNN pipeline achieves an average MSE of 0.390, comparable with 0.396 for deep ensembles, 0.389 for MC dropout, and 0.443 for the full-rank Bayesian model. It uses 63.9\% fewer parameters than MC dropout, 81.9\% fewer than the full-rank model, and 92.8\% fewer than the deep ensemble.

title: On the median of the beta distribution in relation to the median of the gamma distribution
comment: 49 pages, 11 figures. The Lean 4 formalization and Python code that reproduces the figures and numerical checks are in the ancillary files
summary: The median of the beta distribution has no closed form, but it is closely tied to the median of the gamma distribution. Kerman's approximation has the ratio form $g(α)/(g(α)+g(β))$ with $g(x) = x - 1/3$, a lower bound on the gamma median, and it is a lower bound on the beta median for $1/3 < α< β$. The ratio form built from the true gamma median is a tighter lower bound, asymptotically exact as $β\to \infty$. The ratio form built from the Wilson-Hilferty approximation to the gamma median, implicit in a classical approximation to the $F$ distribution but little known as an approximation to the beta median, is an upper bound on the edge $α= 1$ and for large shape parameters. The ratio form that is exact on the lines $α= 1$ and $β= 1$ yields a new approximation to the gamma median, which is an upper bound on it for shape parameter below 1 and a lower bound above 1; no ratio form gives the beta median exactly. For large shape parameters, the logit of the median has an explicit second-order expansion. For small shape parameters, bounds in elementary functions are asymptotically tight, and odds-corrected forms of the low-$α$ asymptote, with an elementary factor that is exact on the edges $α= 1$ and $β= 1$, are, numerically, one-sided bounds within 0.44% of the median that are exact on the lines $α= 1$, $β= 1$, and $α= β$. Steering their exponents with four fitted constants, and interpolating between two ratio forms where both shape parameters exceed 1, gives an approximation in elementary functions that is exact on those lines and numerically within 0.065% of the median over the whole domain. Most of the proofs are machine-verified in Lean 4.

title: Challenge or Pass? A Dynamic Policy for MLB's Automated Ball-Strike System
summary: Under Major League Baseball's automated ball-strike (ABS) challenge system, players must weigh the value of overturning a call against the risk of losing a challenge they may need later. We develop a policy that values an overturn through its effect on expected runs, accounting for the count, outs, and runners on base. Using pitch tracking and game records, we reconstruct challenge opportunities, including calls that players let stand. A Bayesian model represents players' imperfect impressions of pitch location and uses them to estimate overturn probabilities, with uncertainty calibrated from historical challenge decisions. We develop the policy using games before the 2026 All-Star break and evaluate it without refitting on 983 games played afterward. Along the recorded sequence of opportunities, the policy recovers 0.536 modeled correction runs per game across both teams, compared with 0.452 under observed decisions, an improvement of 18.5%. The gain is 0.084 runs per game, with a 95% bootstrap interval of [0.065, 0.103]. The policy makes more challenges and recovers more value per successful review despite a lower overturn rate. title: Proximal R2 Priors for Structured Variance Allocation
summary: Scientific domain knowledge in regression often concerns structural relationships among model terms, which are typically encoded as parameter constraints. Since such relationships rarely hold exactly in practice, prior distributions should encourage them while at the same time retaining support for scientifically plausible departures. Accounting for these relationships becomes more pressing in modern regression, where high-dimensionality is usually present and regularisation is essential. $R^2$ decomposition priors provide an interpretable foundation for regularisation by placing a prior on total explained variance and distributing the implied signal across model terms. We introduce the Proximal R2 prior, which uses proximal relaxations to encode these relationships as soft constraints on the variance allocation. Our formulation yields differentiable posteriors compatible with standard gradient based samplers. Theoretically, we prove that our prior preserves the characteristic marginal properties of global-local shrinkage priors. Moreover, we establish posterior consistency and contraction rates in growing dimensions, showing that the inclusion of structural relationships and proximal methods do not alter the shrinkage properties. title: On the median of the beta distribution in relation to the median of the gamma distribution
comment: 49 pages, 11 figures. The Lean 4 formalization and Python code that reproduces the figures and numerical checks are in the ancillary files
summary: The median of the beta distribution has no closed form, but it is closely tied to the median of the gamma distribution. Kerman's approximation has the ratio form $g(α)/(g(α)+g(β))$ with $g(x) = x - 1/3$, a lower bound on the gamma median, and it is a lower bound on the beta median for $1/3 < α< β$. The ratio form built from the true gamma median is a tighter lower bound, asymptotically exact as $β\to \infty$. The ratio form built from the Wilson-Hilferty approximation to the gamma median, implicit in a classical approximation to the $F$ distribution but little known as an approximation to the beta median, is an upper bound on the edge $α= 1$ and for large shape parameters. The ratio form that is exact on the lines $α= 1$ and $β= 1$ yields a new approximation to the gamma median, which is an upper bound on it for shape parameter below 1 and a lower bound above 1; no ratio form gives the beta median exactly. For large shape parameters, the logit of the median has an explicit second-order expansion. For small shape parameters, bounds in elementary functions are asymptotically tight, and odds-corrected forms of the low-$α$ asymptote, with an elementary factor that is exact on the edges $α= 1$ and $β= 1$, are, numerically, one-sided bounds within 0.44% of the median that are exact on the lines $α= 1$, $β= 1$, and $α= β$. Steering their exponents with four fitted constants, and interpolating between two ratio forms where both shape parameters exceed 1, gives an approximation in elementary functions that is exact on those lines and numerically within 0.065% of the median over the whole domain. Most of the proofs are machine-verified in Lean 4.

title: Independence tests of general spatial point processes based on characteristic functions
summary: Existing nonparametric tests of spatial point process independence typically rely on random shifts to simulate their null distributions. This limits their scope to stationary point processes in rectangular study regions. Attempts to adapt random shift methods to nonrectangular study regions have resulted in significant power loss. We introduce a new type of nonparametric independence tests by taking differences of several characteristic-function-based goodness-of-fit statistics. We develop two null distribution methods for the tests without using random shifts, by making normal or symmetry assumptions on the Mercer's expansion of the test statistics. The methods are applicable to general nonstationary point processes in study regions of any shape. In simulations, our tests based on the symmetric null distribution method have better type I error control and higher power than toroidal cross-$K$ tests in most scenarios where toroidal shifts can be applied. When tested on more general settings given appropriately-fitted marginal distributions, they still have good power and almost always control the type I error well.

title: Zero-Complement Extrapolation: Parameter Recovery and Classification in Severely Imbalanced Logistic Regression under Rank-Deficient Regimes
comment: Submitted to a peer-reviewed journal; 16 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables
summary: Parameter estimation and classification in binary logistic regression deteriorate severely when the number of minority class observations ($n_1$) is smaller than the feature dimension ($p$). title: Fast rates for the classification of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck paths
summary: In binary classification problems, plug-in classifiers can sometimes achieve faster excess risk rates than the underlying estimation rate. In this work, we study a supervised classification problem based on repeated independent observations of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck paths, with both time-homogeneous and time-inhomogeneous drifts. We show that, under a suitable separation condition on the class-dependent drifts, a plug-in classifier attains an excess risk of quadratic order in the corresponding parametric or nonparametric estimation error. The theoretical approach utilizes the Wiener chaos representation and spectral theory to characterize the log-likelihood ratio as a quadratic form of Gaussian random variables, enabling a precise analysis of margin behaviour and deviation results. This extends the fast-rate results from classification problems with linear discriminant models and Gaussian white noise models to dynamical diffusion systems with Gaussian structure.

title: Scaling of Interface Variability in Aerospace Composite Structures: A Multi-scale Stochastic Approach from Local Identification to Panel Response
summary: Quantifying random spatial variations in composite interface properties is an essential prerequisite for the high-fidelity propagation of material properties variabilities through structural numerical models. This study proposes a multi-scale stochastic framework designed to bridge the gap between local interfacial characterization at the coupon scale and the global response of industrial aerospace panels, focusing specifically on the skin-stringer bond line. Building upon previous stochastic modeling and identification methodologies for Mode I fracture, we first extend the likelihood-free Bayesian calibration to Mode II configurations to characterize interfacial stochastic parameters using experimental coupon data. To address the scale-up challenge, we employ a simulation-based Stochastic Finite Element Method (SFEM) to contrast two distinct probabilistic strategies -- spatially uniform variations (Paradigm 2) and spatially correlated random fields (Paradigm 3) -- against the traditional industrial B-basis standard (Paradigm 1). The numerical results reveal a dual mechanism in uncertainty propagation depending on the targeted airframe design criterion. For global performance, such as the ultimate load capacity, a significant scale effect leads to an uncertainty attenuation phenomenon; statistical averaging smooths out local heterogeneities, demonstrating that a computationally efficient spatially uniform approach is sufficient. Conversely, for local integrity, such as the threshold and spatial localization of early damage initiation, the inclusion of spatially correlated random fields becomes indispensable to capture premature degradation driven by local material weak spots. This balanced probabilistic treatment offers a route toward test derisking and predictive uncertainty management in the design of damage-tolerant aerospace composite airframes.

title: An Analysis of High-Dimensional Land-Water Transitions in the Great Lakes via a Bayesian Discrepancy Model for Multinomial Data
summary: Global water-level systems have undergone large changes in recent years. Bayesian hierarchical models are commonly implemented using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods which can be computationally expensive for large datasets. EPR has not been developed for multinomial data, and we extend this class of models to the multinomial setting. Additionally, we explore signal-to-noise covariance properties of discrepancy models, which we expect to be present in our data. We extend EPR to multinomial likelihoods via a stick-breaking construction to analyze water-level changes. Through simulation studies, we compare the proposed multinomial EPR approach with alternative models implemented using Gibbs sampling and the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). We evaluate each approach based on regression parameter estimation, category probability estimation, and computational efficiency. Overall, EPR and INLA achieve substantial reductions in computation time while EPR shows improved metrics in estimation and prediction.
